QF.id: AIFM CIII Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_19

question.text: Ms. Ananya Desai, quant at Sahyadri Stat-Arb Fund, argues that the theoretical CAPM 'market portfolio' is unobservable in practice. What does the chapter recommend as the standard practical substitute, and what risk does this substitution create?

answer.text: Use a risk-free T-bill; no risk since it is observable.
Use a broad-based equity market index as a proxy; an incorrect proxy affects BOTH the beta estimates and the position/slope of the SML used for performance evaluation.
Use the manager's own NAV history; no risk since it is the actual portfolio.
Use a global fixed-income index; creates only a minor tracking error.

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 3.12.1 states: 'Broad based equity market indices are often used as the proxy for such portfolio. There is no unanimity about which proxy to use. An incorrect market proxy will affect both the beta risk measures and the position and slope of the SML that is used to evaluate portfolio performance.' The Trap: (A) contradicts the very definition of the market portfolio (it's risky). (C) is circular. (D) understates the problem and is not the chapter's prescription. Cross-Exam Context: XV, XIX-C/D and XXI-B test Roll's-critique-style proxy-risk arguments. Manager's Pro-Tip: For a Cat III India-centric long-short fund, NIFTY 500 TRI is the cleanest proxy; NIFTY 50 biases beta estimates for mid/small-cap exposures. In your PPM, name the proxy explicitly and disclose the limitation — this is now a standard SEBI inspection talking point.
